rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God brings hidden realities in the human world to light just as He brings concealed things in the greater world to light, exposing hidden states for recompense.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى يخرج ما في العالم الانساني من الخفايا كما يخرج ما في العالم الكبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reveals the concealed conditions people hide so He can requite them; mentioning what they disclose broadens the scope of His knowledge or stresses that hidden and open are equal to Him.
rows.anchor: يظهر ما تخفونه من الأحوال فيجازيكم بها وذكر ماتعلنون لتوسيع دائرة العلم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some infer that the earlier description points to God's complete power, while this description points to His complete knowledge, in which hidden and apparent are equal.
rows.anchor: كلام بعضهم يانه أشير بما تقدم إلى كمال قدرته تعالى وبهذا إلى كمال علمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concealed is mentioned before the disclosed because it suits the preceding mention of hidden things and signals that both are equally known; bringing forth hidden things from heaven comes first because it better fits the context.
rows.anchor: وقدم ( ماتخفون ) لذلك مع مناسبته لما قبله من الخبء وقدم وصفه تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The address may be directed to people generally, Solomon's people, or Bilqis's people.
rows.anchor: والخطاب على ما قيل اما للناس أو لقوم سليمان أو لقوم بلقيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage contains a shift in grammatical person (iltifāt).
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام التفات

rows.speaker: الحرميان والجمهور
rows.claim: The two canonical readers of the Ḥaram and the majority read the verbs in the third person: what they conceal and disclose.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان والجمهور ( مايخفون وما يعلنون ) بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy has a variant reading addressing the hearers directly and ending with God's knowledge of their secret and what they disclose.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف عن أبي أنه قرأ ( ألاتسجدون لله الذي يخرج الخبء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reaching full strength means reaching the point beyond which a person's growth does not increase.
rows.anchor: أي المبلغ الذي لايزيد عليه نشؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiwāʾ means becoming complete and mature, reinforcing and explaining the preceding phrase.
rows.anchor: أي كمل وتم تأكيد وتفسير لما قبله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ sets full strength at ages eighteen to thirty and maturity at thirty to forty, after which decline begins.
rows.anchor: من طريق الكلبي عن أبي صالح عن ابن عباس أنه قال الاشد ما بين الثماني عشر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid sets full strength at thirty-three and maturity at forty; the same is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās and similarly from Qatāda.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد أنه قال الاشد ثلاث وثلاثون سنة والاستواء اربعون سنة وهي رواية عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj once defines full strength as beginning around seventeen and extending to forty.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج مرة بلوغ الاشد من نحو سبع عشرة سنة إلى الاربعين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj also gives the range of thirty to forty for full strength.
rows.anchor: واخرى هو ما بين الثلاثين إلى الاربعين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some prefer the thirty-to-forty range because 46:15 couples reaching full strength with reaching forty; al-Ālūsī says this inference is not free of difficulty.
rows.anchor: واختاره بعضهم هنا وعلل بأن ذلك لموافقته قوله تعالى : ( حتى إدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the general sense: full strength is reaching the limit of bodily power and growth, while maturity is mental balance and perfection; timing varies by region, era, and circumstance.
rows.anchor: والحق أن بلوغ الاشد في الاصل هو الانتهاء إلى حد القوة وذلك وقت انتهاء النمو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses's bodily strength and mental maturity should not be assigned a precise age without a reliable report, although forty is commonly said to be the usual age.
rows.anchor: ولا ينبغي تعيين وقت لذلك في حق موسى عليه السلام إلا بخبر يعول عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poem treats forty as the usual threshold of maturity, and 46:15 offers a supporting parallel.
rows.anchor: نعم اشتهر أن ذلك في الأغلب يكون في سن اربعين وعليه قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī explains the judgment bestowed on Moses as prophethood.
rows.anchor: أي نبوة على ما وري عن السدي أو علما هو من خواص النبوة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others interpret the gift as knowledge belonging to the special qualities of prophethood, or as knowledge of religion and sacred law.
rows.anchor: أو علما هو من خواص النبوة على ما تأول به بعضهم كلامه وعلما بالدين والشريعة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says knowledge means the Torah and judgment means the Sunnah, the practice of the prophets; the verse about what is recited in the houses of the Prophet's wives joins Scripture and wisdom.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف العلم التوراة والحكم السنة وحكمة الانبياء عليهم السلام سنتهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view is that before his mission Moses received the conduct and bearing of wise, learned people and never acted foolishly.
rows.anchor: وقيل آتيناه سيرة الحكماء العلماى وسمتهم قبل البعث فكان عليه السلام لايفعل فعلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī favors the pre-mission conduct-and-knowledge interpretation as it better fits the narrative sequence: Moses's commissioning followed the killing, migration to Midian, return, and Pharaoh's drowning.
rows.anchor: ورجح ما قيل بأنه أوفق لنظم القصة مما تقدم لأن استنباءه عليه السلام بعد وكز القبطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading the earlier gift as prophethood sits uneasily with the statement that benefactors are rewarded, since prophethood is not a reward for deeds.
rows.anchor: على إحسانهم يأبى جمل ما تقدم على النبوة لأنها لا تكون جزاء على العمل

rows.speaker: أصحاب القول الأول
rows.claim: Those who take the gift as prophethood regard it as a summary of the promise to make Moses a messenger after his return to his mother, with later verses detailing it; the conjunction wāw does not require chronological order.
rows.anchor: ومن ذهب إلدى الأول جعل هذا بيانا اجماليا لانجاز الوعد بجعله من المرسلين

rows.speaker: أصحاب القول الأول
rows.claim: On the prophethood reading, what God did for Moses and his mother counts as recompense by a generalizing attribution, and prophethood's higher degrees of nearness may reward righteous action.
rows.anchor: وكون ما فعل بموسى وأمه عليهما السلام جزاء على العمل باعتبار التغليب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophethood itself is not earned as a reward, but a degree of it involving increased nearness to God can be recompense; prophets differ in their nearness to Him.
rows.anchor: أصل النبوة وإن لم تكن جزاء على العمل إلا أن بعض مراتبها وهو ما فيه ميد قرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī further prefers the non-prophethood interpretation because it better suits the promise that Moses's mother would know God's promise true; the implication that every benefactor receives prophethood is no objection to that reading.
rows.anchor: ورجح ما تقدم بكونه أوفق

rows.speaker: من ذهب إلى أن الإيتاء كان قبل الهجرة
rows.claim: If the gift came before migration, it could mean leadership among the Israelites, who turned to Moses in important matters and obeyed his commands, together with useful knowledge.
rows.anchor: ومن ذهب إلى أن الايتاء كان قبل الهجرة قال : يجوز أن يكون المعنى

rows.speaker: من ذهب إلى أن الإيتاء كان قبل الهجرة
rows.claim: This knowledge could come through inspiration or Moses's insight into teachings transmitted from his prophetic ancestors; he could know their beliefs and laws by inspiration or reliable reports.
rows.anchor: وذلك إما بمحض الإلهام أو بتوفيقه لاستنباط دقائق وأسرار مما نقل اليه من كلمات آبائه الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī considers the pre-migration leadership-and-knowledge explanation perhaps preferable to the report quoted in al-Kashshāf and points readers to his discussion near the end of al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: ولعل هذا أولى مما نقله في الكشاف وفي الكلام على أواخر سورة البقرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses turned his face toward Midian; tilqāʾ means the direction opposite or facing it and is originally a verbal noun used adverbially.
rows.anchor: أي صرف وجهه ( تلقاء مدين ( أي ما يقابل جانبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Midian is Shuʿayb's town, named for Midian son of Abraham; it lay outside Pharaoh's dominion, which explains Moses's choice.
rows.anchor: ومدين قرية شعيب سميت باسم مدين بن إبراهيم عليه السلام ولم يكن في سلطان فرعون

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other explanations say Moses headed there because he knew the place or because he was related to its people; the journey from Egypt was eight days.
rows.anchor: وقيل توجه اليها لمعرفته به وقيل لقرابته منه عليهما السلام وكان بينها وبين مصر مسيرة ثمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight middle of the road is the route leading to safety.
rows.anchor: أي وسط الطريق المؤدي إلى النجاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses spoke from reliance on God and confidence in His good guidance, while unfamiliar with the routes.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال عليه السلام ذلك توكلا على الله تعالى وثقة بحسن توفيقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed report says three roads lay ahead: Moses took the middle, while pursuers chose the other two; he remained barefoot for eight nights, eating only leaves.
rows.anchor: فعن ثلاث طرائق فاخذ الوسطى وأخذ طالبوه في الأخريين وقالوا : المريب

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reports that Moses did not arrive until the coverings of his feet had fallen away.
rows.anchor: وعن سعيد بن جبير أنه عليه السلام لم يصل حتى سقط خف قدميه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Gabriel guided Moses to Midian after he set out without knowing the way.
rows.anchor: وروي أن ه عليه السلام أخذ يمشي من غير معرفة فهداه جبريل عليه السلام إلى مدين

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says Moses took side paths and met an angel on horseback with a spear; after Moses bowed in fear, the angel told him to follow and led him to Midian.
rows.anchor: وعن السدي أنه عليه السلام أخذ في بنيات الطريق فجاء ملك على فرس بيده عنزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warada here means reached, not entered or drank; the water means the well from which people drew water, using the place for what occurs there.
rows.anchor: أي وصل اليه وورد والورود بمعنى الدخول وبمعنى الشرب وليس شيء منهما مرادا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlayhi means at the well's rim and watering place.
rows.anchor: أي فوق شفيره ومستقاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umma denotes a large gathering of people of varied kinds; the indefinite form suggests abundance and min al-nās signals the different classes present.
rows.anchor: أي جماعة كثيرة مختلفي الأصناف ويشعر بالقيد الأول التنوين وبالثاني من الناس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Others take min al-nās to disparage the crowd as low people known only by their kind, or to clarify that they were human beings.
rows.anchor: وقيل فائدته تحقير أولئك الجماعة وأنهم لئام لا يعرفون بغير جنسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people apparently watered different kinds of livestock; identifying their animals more narrowly would require transmitted evidence.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنهم كانوا يسقون مواشي مختلفة الأنواع بمعنى أن منهم من كان يسقي إبلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min dūnihim may mean below their position; other explanations are nearby, apart from them, or on the side from which Moses first approached, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya says.
rows.anchor: أي في مكان أسفل من مكانهم وقيل : من قربهم أو من سواهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The daughters' names are variously given as Layā, ʿAbrā, or Sharafā for one, and Ṣafūriyā, Ṣafūrāʾ, or Ṣafīrāʾ for the other; al-Kashshāf calls the younger Ṣafīrāʾ and elder Ṣafrāʾ.
rows.anchor: اسم إحداهما قيل ليا وقيل عبرا وقيل شرفا واسم الأخرى قيل صفوريا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most apparent sense is that they kept their sheep from the well for fear of the stronger shepherds.
rows.anchor: كانتا تمنعان غنمهما عن الماء خوفا من السقاة الأقوياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others say the women held their flocks back from the water out of fear of the powerful watering men.
rows.anchor: خوفا من السقاة الأقوياء قال ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj is cited for the view that they kept their sheep from approaching the well to prevent them mixing with other flocks.
rows.anchor: وقيل تمنعان غنمهما عن التقدم إلى البئر لئلا تختلط بغيرها وحكي ذلك عن الزجاج

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says they were keeping people away from their flock.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : تمنعان الناس عن غنمهما

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says they restrained the sheep so they would not scatter.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : تحبسان غنمهما عن أن تتفرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that the women were warding off spectators' gazes to cover their faces is, in al-Ālūsī's view, untenable.
rows.anchor: وقيل تذودان عن وجوههما نظر الناظرين لتسترهما وهذا كما ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā khaṭbukumā asks what business or need caused their delay and restraint when they were not watering like the others; khaṭb is a verbal noun used for the object sought.
rows.anchor: أي ما مخطوبكما ومطلوبكما مما أنتما عليهما من التأخر والذود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses's question shows that speaking to an unrelated woman is permissible when the matter is pertinent.
rows.anchor: وفي سؤاله عليه السلام إياهما دليل على جواز مكالمة الأجنبية فيما يعني

rows.speaker: شمر
rows.claim: Shammar reads the khāʾ with kasra, taking the question to ask about their husband and why he does not water; al-Ālūsī says the objection raised against this reading is unclear and unanswered.
rows.anchor: وقرأ شمر ( ما خطبكما ) بكسر الخاء قال في البحر : أي من زوجكما

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some defend the common reading by taking khaṭb as the thing sought or requested, comparable to ḥubb meaning the beloved.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : الخطب فيها بمعنى المخطوب والمطلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women describe their usual practice: they wait until the shepherds send their animals away because they cannot compete with them, rather than saying they will not water on that particular day until then.
rows.anchor: أي عادتنا أن لانسقي حتى يصرف الرعاة مواشيهم بعد ريها عن الماء عجزا

rows.speaker: ابن مصرف
rows.claim: Ibn Muṣarrif reads the nūn with ḍamma, using the causative form asqā instead of the common form saqā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مصرف ( لانسقي ) نضم النون من الاسقاء

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAmr, along with the other listed readers, read yuṣdira with an open yāʾ and ḍamma on dāl, meaning the shepherds depart with their flocks.
rows.anchor: والعربيان : ابن عامر وأبو عمرو ( يصدر ) بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One explanation contrasts the readings: the open-yāʾ reading emphasizes the women's modesty and avoidance of men, while the ḍamma-yāʾ reading has the shepherds drive the animals off without implying that the men themselves leave.
rows.anchor: فأجيب بأن قراءة يصدر بفتح الياء تدل على فرط حيائها وتواريهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other recitations pronounce the consonant as pure zāy or as a sound between ṣād and zāy.
rows.anchor: وقريء بزاي خالصة وبحرف بين الصاد والزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant has ḍamma on rāʾ; the familiar plural pattern faʿāl has kasra, while ḍamma is irregular and may be a collective noun, an original plural, or a plural with a changed vowel.
rows.anchor: وقريء الرعاء بضم الراء والمعروف في صيغ الجمع فعال بكسر الفاء

rows.speaker: صدر الأفاضل
rows.claim: A cited mnemonic poem lists exceptional fuʿāl plurals such as ربّاب، فرار، تؤام، عرام، عراق، رخال، ظؤار، and بساط; al-Ālūsī says its author is Ṣadr al-Afāḍil, not al-Zamakhsharī as sometimes claimed.
rows.anchor: وقد نظمها صدر الأفاضل لا الزمخشري على الأصح بقوله : ما سمعنا كلما غير ثمان

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān also considers the common plural riʿāʾ non-analogical: an agent adjective rāʿin would regularly pluralize as quḍāt, not this form.
rows.anchor: وذهب أبو حيان إلى أن الرعاء في قراءة الجمهور ليس بقياس أيضا قال : لأنه جمع راع

rows.speaker: عياش عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: ʿAyyāsh from Abū ʿAmr reads riʿāʾ with fatḥa on rāʾ, either as a verbal noun used adjectivally for singular and plural or with an omitted muḍāf meaning the people of herding.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عياش عن أبي عمرو الرعاء بفتح الراء وهو مصدر أقيم مقام الصفة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the women excused themselves as weak and modest, unable to compete with men, with no man to help and an aged, enfeebled father, so they had to wait until the others finished.
rows.anchor: كأنهما قالتا : إنا امرأتان ضعيفتان مستورتان لا نقدر على مساجلة الرجال

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say Moses's gracious question sought their need and implicitly offered help; the women's reply supplied the reason for their delay and indirectly requested assistance.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم أنه عليه السلام اخرج السؤال على ما يقتضيه كرمه ورحمته بالضعفاء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view finds no explicit statement of weakness: the words signal modesty, and their father handled the task before age and frailty forced the daughters to take it up.
rows.anchor: وقيل : ليس في الكلام ما يدل على ضعفهما بل فيه أمارات على حيائهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī's preferred explanation is that they conveyed inability to compete because of both weakness and their natural modesty, even though the wording does not explicitly state weakness.
rows.anchor: ولعل الأولى أن يقال : إنهما أرادتا إظهار العجز عن المساجلة للضعف ولما جبلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about their father may coordinate with an omitted clause or function circumstantially: they wait until the shepherds depart while their father is old.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن تكون حالا أي نترك السقي حتى يصدر الرعاء والحال أبونا شيخ كبير

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify the women's father as the prophet Shuʿayb.
rows.anchor: وأبوهما عند أكثر المفسرين شعيب عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet's allowing his daughters to water sheep is not forbidden by religion; judgments of propriety vary with custom, between Bedouin and urban life, and with necessity.
rows.anchor: أن الأمر في نفسه ليس بمحظور فالدين لا يأباه وأما المروءة فالناس مختلفون

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda, in reports collected by Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abī Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, says Moses's employer was Athrūn, Shuʿayb's nephew; Abū Ḥayyān gives Hārūn instead of Athrūn, and al-Ḥasan gives Marwān.
rows.anchor: فأخرج سعيد بن منصور وابن أبي شيبة وابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم عن أبي عبيدة

rows.speaker: وهب وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī transmits from Wahb and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr a version identifying the father as Shuʿayb's nephew, like Abū ʿUbayda's view as quoted by Abū Ḥayyān.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبرسي عن وهب وسعيد بن جبير نحو ما حكاه أبو حيان عن أبي عبيدة

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says he had heard that the father was Shuʿayb's nephew named Raʿāwīl; a reliable informant said scripture calls him Yathrūn, priest or learned authority of Midian.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن ابن جريج أنه قال بلغني أن أبا الامرأتين ابن أخي شعيب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to call the employer Yathrib, master of Midian, and in another version Yathrūn, without specifying a relationship to Shuʿayb.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير عن ابن عباس أنه قال الذي استأجر موسى عليه السلام يثرب صاحب مدين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other possibilities are that the man named in those reports was Shuʿayb's nephew or an unrelated person, or that the father was a righteous man unrelated to Shuʿayb.
rows.anchor: فيحتمل أن المسمى بما فيها ابن اخيه ويحتمل أنه رجل أجنبي عنه فقد قيل

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabrisī reports a view that Yathrūn was Shuʿayb himself; a person of the People of the Book told al-Ālūsī that their form is Yathro without final nūn.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبرسي عن بعضهم أن يثرون اسم شعيب وقد أخبرني بعض أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: التوراة
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī's translation of Exodus 2 says Midian's priest had seven daughters, whom Moses helped water after shepherds drove them off; Exodus 3 calls Moses shepherd to Jethro, his father-in-law and priest of Midian.
rows.anchor: وكان لامام مدين سبع بنات فجاءت ودلت وملأت الاحواض لسقي غنم أبيهن

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A view cited in al-Baḥr says the daughters' uncle owned the flock and arranged the marriage, but they called him father because he was like one to them.
rows.anchor: قيل : كان عمها صاحب الغنم وهو المزوج عبرت عنه بالأب إذ كان بمثابته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says such historical claims require a reliable report, notes the reports conflict without a clear strongest version, and follows the majority view that their actual father was Shuʿayb until evidence warrants departure.
rows.anchor: فالمدار في قبول شيء من ذلك خبر يعول عليه والاخبار التي وقفنا عليها في هذا المطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father’s statement is an explanatory resumption answering what he said after hearing his daughter; its emphatic form conveys strong desire for the proposal.
rows.anchor: استئناف بياني كأنه قيل : فما قال أبوها بعد أن سمع كلامها فقيل : قال إني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative hint may imply he had other daughters; al-Mundhir reports four younger sisters, while al-Biqāʿī says seven as in the Torah and al-Kashshāf sees evidence for that.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله ( هاتين ) إيماء إلى أنه كانت له بنات أخر غيرهما وقد أخرج ابن المنذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that the demonstrative proves other daughters is not decisive: pointing could distinguish these two from other known daughters; al-Ālūsī says the dispute is not worth pressing.
rows.anchor: واعترض بأنه لا دلالة فيه على ما ذكر إذ يكفي في الحاجة إلى الاشارة

rows.speaker: ورش وأحمد بن موسى عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: Warsh and Aḥmad ibn Mūsā from Abū ʿAmr read the verb with the hamza omitted.
rows.anchor: أحمد بن موسى عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condition that Moses work for him can be circumstantial to the object of the marriage verb, meaning the marriage is conditional on it, or circumstantial to its subject, as Abū al-Baqāʾ says.
rows.anchor: في موضع الحال من مفعول ( أنكحك ) أي مشروطا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʾjurnī can mean that Moses hires himself out to the father, with thamanī ḥijaj specifying the period; the verb then takes one object.
rows.anchor: وتأجرني من أجرته كنت له أجيرا كقولك أبوته كنت له أبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, taʾjurnī can mean reward me, from God's rewarding someone: it takes two objects, with an omitted noun meaning tending the sheep for eight years as the marriage payment.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون تأجرني بمعنى تثيبني من أجره تعالى على ما فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the reward sense, the phrase may modify the verb after an omitted object: Moses compensates the father with his service or labor over eight years.
rows.anchor: وجوز على هذا المعنى أن يكون ظرفا لتأجرني أيضا بحذف المفعول

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad distinguishes ajartu without lengthening from ājartu with lengthening, says the short form is more common, and on that analysis a second object is omitted: Moses's self.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن المبرد أنه يقال : أجرت داري ومملوكي غير مدود وآجرت ممدودا

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib says ajara views the act from one party's perspective and ājara from both parties'; both return to the same meaning, and the lexicons list both forms.
rows.anchor: الراغب : يقال أجرت زيدا إذا اعتبر فعل أحدهما

rows.speaker: تحفة المحتاج
rows.claim: Tuḥfat al-Muḥtāj gives the forms for hiring and says ijāra, the noun for the wage, is most eloquent with kasra on its hamza before becoming the conventional term for the contract; ḥijaj means years.
rows.anchor: وفيها أن الاجارة بتثليث الهمزة والكسر أفصح لغة اسم للاجرة ثم اشتهرت في العقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥijaj is the plural of ḥijja, meaning a year.
rows.anchor: والحجج جمع حجة بالكسر السنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Moses completes ten years of service, the extra two are a voluntary favor from him, not an obligation imposed by the father.
rows.anchor: فمن عندك أي فهو من عندك من طريق التفضل لا من عندي بطريق الالزام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father does not intend to burden Moses by requiring all ten years, closely policing the schedule, or demanding exhaustive completion of every task.
rows.anchor: بالزام إتمام العشر والمناقشة في مراعاة الأوقات واستيفاء الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The noun for hardship derives from splitting something into two: what is hard divides the mind over whether to bear it.
rows.anchor: واشتقاق المشقة وهي ما يصعب تحمله من الشق بفتح الشين وهو فصل الشيء

words: سَتَجِدُنِىٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being among the صالحين means treating Moses well, showing gentleness, and keeping the agreement.
rows.anchor: في حسن المعاملة ولين الجانب والوفاء بالعهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father invokes God's will for blessing and entrusts the matter to divine enabling; he is not making his righteousness conditional on permission to act unrighteously.
rows.anchor: ومراد شعيب عليه السلام بالاستثناء التبرك به وتفويض أمره إلى توفيقه تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the father's established righteousness makes a conditional statement unnecessary; al-Ālūsī compares al-Shāfiʿī's statement, I am a believer, God willing.
rows.anchor: قول الشافعي : أنا مؤمن إن شاء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anything people attain among worldly affairs and means is a temporary use and adornment; matāʿ signals brevity, the contrast with abqā stresses it, and dunyā suggests lowliness and short duration.
rows.anchor: فهو شيء شأنه أن يتمتع به ويتزين به أياما قلائل ويشعر بالقلة لفظ المتاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What is with God means the reward in Paradise; it is intrinsically better as pure pleasure and complete joy, and more lasting because eternal, unlike the finite world.
rows.anchor: لأنه لذة خالصة وبهجة كاملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question urges reflection on the obvious choice: do not trade the lower for the better, fear losing worldly possessions, and refuse guidance that leads to God's reward based on that hypothetical fear.
rows.anchor: أي ألا تتفكرون فلا تفعلون هذا الأمر الواضح فتستبدلون الذي هو أدنى

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr reads yaʿqilūn in the third person; the shift makes the admonition stronger by implying that they are too senseless to merit direct address.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو يعقلون بياء الغيبة على الالتفات وهو أبلغ في الموعظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant reads matāʿan in the accusative as a verbal noun and al-ḥayāta as a temporal adverb, meaning they enjoy it in worldly life.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( فمتاعا الحياة الدنيا ) أي فتتمتعون به في الحياة الدنيا

words: وَمَا كُنتَ تَتْلُوا۟ مِن قَبْلِهِۦ مِن كِتَٰبٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before revelation of the Book, Muhammad could not recite any book; alternatively, reciting and writing books had not been his custom.
rows.anchor: أي وما كنت من قبل إنزالنا إليك الكتاب تقدر على أن تتلو ( من كتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning the right hand vividly reinforces the literal denial of writing, like saying I saw with my eye, and rules out a figurative reading.
rows.anchor: وذكر اليمين زيادة تصوير لما نفى عنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم من الخط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had Muhammad been able or accustomed to read and write, Meccan polytheists would have suspected he copied earlier books; since he was unlettered, they had no grounds, and such a detailed book could not be learned without prolonged, visible study.
rows.anchor: لو كنت ممن يقدر على التلاوة والخط أو ممن يعتادها لأرتاب مشركو مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are called falsifiers because they doubted and disbelieved; one explanation ties this to their doubt despite Muhammad's actual illiteracy, while another says even if he were literate their doubt would invalidate them because illiteracy is only one proof among several.
rows.anchor: ووصف مشركي مكة بالأبطال بإعتبار إرتيابهم وكفرهم وهو عليه الصلاة والسلام أمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second analysis calls them falsifiers whether or not Muhammad was unlettered: literacy would remove only one aspect of the miracle, while the remaining proofs suffice, as with doubters of non-literate prophets.
rows.anchor: وأما كونهم كذلك بالإعتبار الثاني فلأن غاية ما يلزم من عدم أميته صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf treats the conditional as a hypothetical illustration showing that the miracle is the basis of the argument; illiteracy is not the only proof, and those who deny the truth are falsifiers.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف هذا فرض وتمثيل دلالة على أن مدار الأمر على المعجز

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the falsifiers as the polytheists of Mecca; al-Ālūsī says this is the stronger interpretation.
rows.anchor: وكون المراد بالمبطلين مشركي مكة هو المروى عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda identifies the falsifiers as the People of the Book, who would doubt because their scripture describes Muhammad as unlettered.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة : هم أهل الكتاب أي لو كنت تتلو من قبل أو تخط لأرتاب

rows.speaker: البغوي
rows.claim: Al-Baghawī's al-Tahdhīb chooses as the sounder view that the Prophet never learned to write after his mission either.
rows.anchor: فقيل : إنه عليه الصلاة والسلام لم يكن يحسن الكتاب وأختاره البغوي في التهذيب

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some claim that after the Qur'an was revealed, Islam spread, and the doubt had become prominent, the Prophet learned writing, his earlier inability having served the miracle.
rows.anchor: بعضهم أنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن أبي شيبة وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Shayba and others transmit that the Prophet did not die until he had written and read.
rows.anchor: أبي شيبة وغيره ما مات
